A deciduous branching and bony structure on the head of deer (Cervidae), normally in pairs, grown and shed each year.

resembling antlers

antonym.e: From French antonyme (1840s and 1850s), which was modeled on earlier synonyme and influenced by the etymons of Ancient Greek ἀντωνυμία (antōnumía, “pronoun”); credit for popularization of the French loanword's naturalization into English is given principally to Charles John Smith and his 1867 book Synonyms and Antonyms: Or, Kindred Words and Their Opposites. Collected and Contrasted. By surface analysis, ant- + -onym.

s.d: a word that expresses a meaning opposed to the meaning of another word, in which case the two words are antonyms of each other
x: to him the antonym of ‘gay’ was ‘depressed’

s.d: A word which has the opposite (averted or inverted) meaning of another word.
x: “Rich” is an antonym of “poor”; “full” is an antonym of “empty”.

s.d: A word which has the opposite (averted or inverted) meaning of another word.: A word that describes one end of a scale, while its opposite describes the other end, such as large versus small; a gradable antonym.
x: "The word 'boom' always makes me uneasy because the antonym of it is bust," said Patrick Jankowski, vice president of research at the Greater Houston Partnership. "Houston is not in a boom -- it is on a new path."

Any amphibian of the order Anura: any frog (narrow sense) or toad.
relating to frogs and toads
Of or relating to the order Anura.
x: As a further illustration, we may take the results of experiments in which a Urodele organiser (from Triton alpestris) is grafted into an Anuran embryo (Bufo vulgaris).

a small bone in the middle ear between the malleus and the stapes

x:
My heart is as an anvil unto sorrow,
Which beats upon it like the Cyclops’ hammers […]

I saw a smith stand with his hammer, thus,
The whilst his iron did on the anvil cool,
With open mouth swallowing a tailor’s news […]

s.d: The incus bone in the middle ear.
A stone or other hard surface used by a bird for breaking the shells of snails.
The non-moving surface of a micrometer against which the item to be measured is placed.
A horizontal-topped mass of cloud, shaped like a blacksmith's anvil, that forms before a thunderstorm.

Which I commit, not to your patronage,
But skill and Art […]
The Family Tang caus’d an Iron Pillar to be erected there of three Rods high, and of a proportionable thickness, Anvil’d out of an intire Piece.

anxiety.e: Borrowed from Latin ānxietās, from ānxius (“anxious, solicitous, distressed, troubled”), from angō (“to distress, trouble”), akin to Ancient Greek ἄγχω (ánkhō, “to choke”). Equivalent to anxious + -ety. See anger; angst.

s.d: (psychiatry) a relatively permanent state of worry and nervousness occurring in a variety of mental disorders, usually accompanied by compulsive behavior or attacks of panic
a vague unpleasant emotion that is experienced in anticipation of some (usually ill-defined) misfortune
(uncountable) An unpleasant state of mental uneasiness, nervousness, apprehension and obsession or concern about some uncertain event.

feel anxiety

s.d: (uncountable) An uneasy or distressing desire (for something). Endeavor (to please).

s.d: a sudden acute episode of intense anxiety and feelings of panic
a cover term for a variety of mental disorders in which severe anxiety is a salient symptom

x: "Elliot, Clinton asserts that he has no desire to end your relationship. Your fears are therefore unfounded. We are directing you to seek professional help for your anxiety disorder."

s.d: Accompanied with, or causing, anxiety; worrying.

s.d: Earnestly desirous.

s.d: to any degree or extent

s.d: To even the slightest extent; at all.
x: 'That wouldn't surprise me any.'

s.d: To even the slightest extent; at all.: Used before different, before comparatives with more and less, and idiomatically before other comparatives, generally in interrogative, hypothetical, or negative contexts.
x: If you get any taller, you'll start having to duck through doorways!
Is she any less enthused now that it's raining?

s.d: (US) To even the slightest extent; at all.: Used to modify a verb, generally a finite verb or a non-finite verb in object position.
x: That doesn't bother me any.

s.d: One at all; at least one; at least one kind of; some; a positive quantity of.

s.d: A/an, each or some, no matter its/their identity or nature.
x: Choose any item you want.

s.d: An unspecified but imminent (second, minute, day etc.).

s.d: Any thing(s) or person(s).

s.d: In negative or interrogative constructions: from a given time onwards.
